added_lines: RESPONSE : The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want . GOSPEL READING : Matthew 25:31-46 Jesus said to his disciples: ‘When the Son of Man comes in his glory, escorted by all the angels, then he will take his seat on his throne of glory. All the nations will be assembled before him and he will separate men one from another as the shepherd separates sheep from goats. He will place the sheep on his right hand and the goats on his left. Then the King will say to those on his right hand, “Come, you whom my Father has blessed, take for your heritage the kingdom prepared for you since the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you made me welcome; naked and you clothed me, sick and you visited me, in prison and you came to see me. ” Then the virtuous will say to him in reply , “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you; or thirsty and give you drink? When did we see you a stranger and make you welcome; naked and clothe you; sick or in prison and go to see you? ” And the King will answer, “I tell you solemnly, in so far as you did this to one of the least of these brothers of mine, you did it to me. ” Next he will say to those on his left hand, “Go away from me, with your curse upon you, to the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you never gave me food; I was thirsty and you never gave me anything to drink; I was a stranger and you never made me welcome, naked and you never clothed me, sick and in prison and you never visited me. ” Then it will be their turn to ask , “Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, a stranger or naked, sick or in prison, and did not come to your help? ” Then he will answer , “I tell you solemnly, in so far as you neglected to do this to one of the least of these, you neglected to do it to me. ” And they will go away to eternal punishment, and the virtuous to eternal life. ’ The Gospel of the Lord Praise to you, Lord Jesus Christ. A KING WHO SERVES When we hear the word king, we think of power and palaces. Jesus turns that upside down. In today’s Gospel, the King stands before us in the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner. He tells us, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me ”. His Kingdom is not built on force. It is built on love shown in small, everyday acts of kindness . In the First Reading, God says through Ezekiel, “I myself will look after my sheep. ” Our King is a shepherd who searches for the lost, binds up the in- jured, and strengthens the weak. We see that kingship here in Longford every week, when someone visits a lonely neighbour, serves in this Cathedral, or shares food with someone who has little. St Paul reminds us that Christ will hand over the Kingdom to the Father when even death is destroyed. That means our work of love is not wasted. Every act of mercy and forgiveness is part of building His Kingdom here on earth. As this Church year ends, Christ the King asks us one question: Where did you find Me this week? Let us answer Him not only with our words in this Cathedral, but with our hands and hearts outside it, by serving the least among us as if we were serving Christ himself. Longford (Templemichael)

, King of the Universe A 26 | Le beatae. aoeoh The story of Saint Louis IX, King of France is the ultimate reflection of Christ’s kingly nature paired with absolute, radical humility toward the poor, Louis possessed near total, absolute earthly power, yet he was renowned for his unshakeable jusuce. He understood perfectly that his crown belonged to Christ, and therefore, his primary duty as a king was to be a servant to the humblest of his subjects.

The King on His Knees Every single day, King Louis invited well over a hundred poor people into his royal palace in Paris to be fed. He did not simply pay servants to feed them from a distance. Instead, he would personally wear a simple apron, carry the heavy platters from the kitchen, and serve the poor beggars at the tables. He would carve their meat, pour their wine, and hand them bread. Belore they departed, the King of France would kneel on the stone floor, wash their dirty, calloused feet, and kiss them. His ministers and nobles were often embarrassed by this behaviour. “Vhey argued that it was beneath the dignity of the Crown and that it made the monarchy look weak. Louis calmly replied to them: "The poor are my masters. Do not think that I lose any dignity by serving those who represent Christ Himself. A king is never more royal than when he serves the King of Kings in His poor." The Leper in the Woods On one occasion, while travelling through lus kingdom with his royal retinue, Louis encountered a man suffering from advanced leprosy, “The man's face was disfigured, his skin was covered in weeping sores, and he was ringing a bell to warn people to stay away, as was required by law. The royal guards immediately moved to push the leper into the woods to protect the King from the sight and the risk of infection. Louis stopped his horse. He dismounted, brushed past his protesting guards, and walked directly up to the terrified leper. “The King knelt in the mud, took the leper's bandaged hands into his own, and kissed them. He then pulled a pouch of gold coms from his belt, placed it gently in the man's hands, and spoke words ol comfort to him. He showed his court that a true leader does not use power to distance himself from human suflering, but to bridge the gap. The Ultimate Final Instructions

Belore he died, King Louis wrote a famous letter of instruction to his son, who would inherit the throne. His final advice perfectly encapsulates the heart ol this Sunday's Gospel: "Be generous to the poor, and help them with all your heart. Comfort them in their distress. Never oppress your people, but defend them with justice. And remember . When you serve the poor. you serve the King of Kings. For He said: “In so far as you did this to the poorest of my servants . you did this to me.” Unfortunately, his successors just like most rulers . did not follow his advice.

Sunday 15th November This Sunday’s first reading from The Book of Proverbs speaks about the perfect wife nurturing her household.
It is an image of what God has entrusted to us.

In the Gospel the talents refer to our share if the life of Grace– our share in the work of creation, our sharing in the building up of the kingdom of God, and our responsibility for nurturing all those around us.
St Thomas Aquinas writes: “ creation is none other than the relation of creature to the creator. ” 2a.
We depend on God for everything-life, faith the world, beauty and each other.
